profiles.profile: Raised before the flop exactly once in 51 hands, which by Lily's standards counts as a wild outburst. Plays four hands in ten and then mostly calls her way through them, letting other people decide how much the hand costs.

Zero raises in 51 hands, in for more than half of them, and reaching showdown only a quarter of the time, so the chips go in early and leave quietly. A steady stream of small donations to the flop, then a change of heart.

Sees 57% of flops and then almost never reaches the showdown, which means a lot of chips are being paid for a peek and then abandoned. Raises before the flop about once in eight hands and calls the rest of the time, like buying a ticket to every film and walking out at the trailers.

Plays 71% of hands, and from the toughest early seats a staggering 93%, which means folding is basically a rumour. Once the flop arrives the betting stops entirely, so every hand becomes a long quiet walk to find out who won.

One of the few here who folds when someone bets at them, which is quietly worth money. Plays more hands from the seats where it's hardest to play them and fewer from the seats where it's easy, like driving with the handbrake on downhill.
Quietly the most balanced player here, folding plenty and betting when it's their turn to. Boring in a profitable way, which in this room is practically a personality disorder.
Zero raises in 64 hands. Plays two thirds of them and goes to showdown 64% of the time, which is less a strategy than a promise that you will always find out what he had.

Raises more than anyone here and actually bets the flop when it checks to them, which at this table counts as witchcraft. Still plays nearly half of everything dealt, so the aggression comes bundled with a lot of hands that didn't need to be there.
Twenty-four hands in and already playing two thirds of them while raising almost never. Somehow up a healthy pile of chips, which is exactly the kind of early evidence that gets expensive later.

Plays 61% of hands and raises before the flop about once every twenty, which is less a strategy than an open invitation. Sees more flops than anyone except Shaw-Ern, and once there mostly checks and hopes, like a passenger who insists on riding in every car but never touching the wheel.

Reasonably sensible by the standards of this room, and one of the few who actually bets the flop after raising. Then plays more hands from the worst seat than the best one, which undoes some of the good work.
